system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2206-01-17 11:30:00 to 2206-01-18 18:18:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder, was admitted due to darker red output from his bilateral nephrostomy tubes and absent drainage from the right tube. He had no pain or fever. He was recently discharged after treatment for urosepsis and was continuing oral ciprofloxacin. Imaging and nephrostogram revealed a clogged right tube and bleeding from the left nephrostomy tract. Both tubes were replaced, with the left upsized to improve drainage and reduce bleeding. He was observed overnight, remained stable, and his hemoglobin showed an expected post-procedure drop. He was discharged home with instructions to continue antibiotics, monitor tube output, and complete a CBC in one week. Wound care for existing pressure ulcers was emphasized.
problems: Other complication of continent stoma of urinary tract
Surgical operation with formation of external stoma as the cause of abnormal reaction of the patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at the time of the procedure
Pressure ulcer of right buttock, stage 2
Pressure ulcer of other site, stage 2
Age-related osteoporosis without current pathological fracture
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Acquired absence of other specified parts of digestive tract

Discharge Instructions:
NEPHROSTOMY TUBE INSTRUCTIONS FOR CARE---FOR ___ & FAMILY:

-Please leave the PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROSTOMY (PCN) tube to 
external gravity drainage and flush forward with 10 mL normal 
saline solution twice daily to maintain tube patency. Please 
monitor and record urine output from the PCN tube as directed 
frequently throughout the day.

Catheter flushing: If there are excessive blood clots or debris 
or thick urine within the connecting tubing, this can also be 
flushed as needed to clear from the stopcock into the drainage 
bag.

Change dressing daily. Gently cleanse around the skin entry site 
of the catheter with povidone iodine or dilute hydrogen 
peroxide. Dry and apply sterile gauze dressing.

Catheter security: a) Every shift, check to be sure the 
catheter, the connecting tubing and the drainage bag are 
securely attached to the patient and are not kinked. b) If the 
catheter appears to be pulling, please notify Interventional 
Radiology. c) If the catheter pulls out, please notify 
Interventional Radiology with in 8 hours. SAVE THE CATHETER for 
us to inspect. Do not throw it away.

Call Angio for ANY catheter related questions or problems. 
___ or Fellow/Resident (___)

Catheter is attached to drainage bag for external drainage; 
please measure and record the netoutput every shift (or more 
often if the urine output is high).

---You will be discharged home with visiting nurse services to 
facilitate your care of your PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROSTOMY TUBE.

-please also reference the provided educational handout on 
caring for your nephrostomy tube (provided by nursing)

-No vigorous physical activity for 2 weeks AND while nephrostomy 
tube is in place

-Expect to see occasional blood in your urine and to experience 
urgency and frequency over the next month.

-The kidney stone may or may not have been removed AND/or there 
may fragments/others still in the process of passing.

-You may experience some pain associated with spasm of your 
ureter. This is normal. Take the narcotic pain medication as 
prescribed if additional pain relief is needed.
-Tylenol should be your first line pain medication, a narcotic 
pain medication has beenprescribed for breakthrough pain >4. 
Replace Tylenol with narcotic pain medication.

-Max daily Tylenol (acetaminophen) dose is 4 grams from ALL 
sources,
note that narcotic pain medication also contains Tylenol

-Make sure you drink plenty of fluids to help keep yourself 
hydrated and facilitate passage of stone fragments.

-You may shower but do not bathe or immerse in water.

-Do not drive or drink alcohol while taking narcotics or operate 
dangerous machinery

-Colace has been prescribed to avoid post surgical constipation 
and constipation related tonarcotic pain medication. Discontinue 
if loose stool or diarrhea develops.  Colace is a stool 
softener, NOT a laxative

-Resume all of your pre-admission medications EXCEPT as 
otherwise noted.

-Call your urologists office for follow-up AND if you have any 
questions.  ALWAYS call to discuss your 
post-hospitalization/post-operative course with your primary 
care physician; especially if there have been changes to your 
medications.

-You may have been given a course of antibiotics--please 
complete the course as instructed.

-resume your regular home diet and remember to drink plenty of 
fluids to keep hydrated and to prevent constipation

-___ medical attention for fevers (temp>101.5), worsening pain, 
drainage or excessive
bleeding from incision, chest pain or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___, your urology doctor. You're here today for your right percutaneous nephrolithotomy to treat the kidney stone. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi doctor. I’m a bit nervous, but okay. The stone’s been causing a lot of discomfort lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The procedure is minimally invasive and should help relieve the blockage. We’ll place a small tube in your kidney to remove the stone fragments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have another nephrostomy tube like before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a temporary one on the right side. It will drain urine and any stone fragments. The left tube is still in place from your last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And will I be in pain afterward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some discomfort is normal. We’ll start with IV pain meds and switch to oral ones tomorrow. You’ll have acetaminophen and a narcotic for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get IV antibiotics for 24 hours to prevent infection. After that, you’ll take fosfomycin once by mouth before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember taking cipro before. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of past infections with resistant bacteria, we’re using fosfomycin this time—it works well for your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll take you to the operating room shortly. The procedure should take a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The procedure went well. We used fluoroscopy to guide the instruments and removed the stone fragments. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the tube in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the right nephrostomy tube is in place and draining. Your left tube and suprapubic catheter are also working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A little is expected. We’ll monitor it. You’re on IV pain meds now and will start drinking fluids soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the chest X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a portable chest X-ray after surgery. Your lungs look clear, no fluid or infection. Everything is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I took Tylenol this morning and it helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We checked your labs this morning—your hemoglobin is stable, and kidney function is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fever, and your white blood cell count is normal. You finished the IV antibiotics, so you’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you tolerated your diet yesterday, so keep with your regular home diet. Drink plenty of fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll clamp it this morning to see if your kidney can drain on its own. If you stay pain-free, we’ll remove it this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube has been clamped for a couple of hours. Any pain or discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll remove the right nephrostomy tube now. The left one stays for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tube is out. The site is clean and not bleeding. You’re doing very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep the left nephrostomy tube for now. Flush it twice daily with saline, change the dressing every day, and monitor urine output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Tylenol first. If pain is above 4, take the narcotic. But don’t exceed 4 grams of Tylenol a day—remember it’s in the narcotic too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a visiting nurse to help with the tube. And you’re scheduled for the left-side procedure in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—call if you have fever over 101.5, worsening pain, heavy bleeding, or trouble breathing. And don’t drive while on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Pain still controlled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just mild soreness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. The nurse will review all instructions again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’ll see you soon for the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Bye for now.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder managed with a suprapubic catheter, was admitted for a right percutaneous nephrolithotomy due to bilateral kidney stones. The procedure was performed without complications, and a temporary nephrostomy tube was placed on the right side. He received intravenous antibiotics for 24 hours and was transitioned to oral pain control with acetaminophen and a narcotic for breakthrough pain. The right nephrostomy tube was clamped and subsequently removed on postoperative day one after he remained pain-free. He tolerated a regular diet, had stable labs, and no signs of infection. He was discharged home with instructions to care for the remaining left nephrostomy tube, continue fosfomycin, monitor for complications, and prepare for the left-sided procedure in the coming weeks.
